The Best Roads for Classic Motorcycles in the UK

There is a particular kind of joy in riding a classic or retro motorcycle, and it has nothing to do with going fast. The best roads for classic motorcycles in the UK are the ones that let you savour the machine beneath you, roads with a relaxed rhythm, scenery that rewards a slower pace and villages spaced perfectly for the frequent stops that older bikes and their riders both appreciate. Whether you are aboard a genuine vintage machine or a modern retro like a Royal Enfield or a Triumph Bonneville, these routes are chosen to suit lower speeds, gentler gradients and a day built around the pleasure of the ride rather than the destination.

A classic bike changes how you travel. You plan around fuel range, you stop when the machine wants a rest, and you avoid sustained high-speed motorway blasts that leave an air-cooled engine and a hard-tail rider equally rattled. My guide to how to tour on a classic or retro bike covers the mechanical side. Here I want to share the roads themselves, the heritage routes that make a classic sing.

The Cotswolds Heritage Run (A429 and B4632)

Nowhere in England suits a classic motorcycle quite like the Cotswolds. The honey-stone villages, the unhurried limits and the gently undulating roads seem to have been designed with a Bonneville in mind. The A429 Fosse Way gives you long relaxed straights and easy bends, while the B4632 around Winchcombe and Broadway adds scenic ridge-top views. A leisurely 60-mile loop taking in Stow-on-the-Wold, Bourton-on-the-Water and Broadway breaks neatly into short legs with a tearoom at every turn.

This is riding at its most civilised. You are rarely doing more than 50mph, the surfaces are generally kind, and there is always somewhere charming to pull over and let the engine cool while you admire the machine. My full Cotswolds touring routes guide maps the whole area. Park at Bourton, prop the bike on its stand and enjoy the admiring glances from passers-by.

Yorkshire Dales Gentle Grand Tour

The Yorkshire Dales offer some of the most beautiful riding in Britain, and while the region has its dramatic passes, there is a wealth of relaxed dale-bottom roads that suit a classic perfectly. The B6160 through Wharfedale, running from Bolton Abbey up through Kettlewell, is a gorgeous unhurried ribbon of tarmac following the river with drystone walls and green fells on either side. Link it with the roads around Grassington and Malham for a 70-mile day of pure scenic pleasure.

Keep the legs short and the stops frequent. Grassington has a lovely cobbled square with cafes, and Kettlewell is a classic Dales village made for a mid-ride brew. Because you are following the valley floors rather than hauling over the tops, the gradients stay gentle and the pace stays relaxed. My Yorkshire Dales routes guide has the full picture including the more demanding passes for another day.

A classic motorcycle teaches you patience, and the best roads reward it. Stop chasing the horizon and start noticing the drystone walls, the church towers and the way the light falls on the fells. That is what riding a classic is really about.

The New Forest and Avon Valley

For a shorter, softer day, the New Forest and the neighbouring Avon Valley are made for classic bikes. The low limits and quiet roads mean an older machine is never straining, and the flat-to-gently-rolling terrain is kind to bikes with modest brakes and drum-braked front ends. A 45-mile loop from Lyndhurst down to Beaulieu and out along the Avon Valley towards Ringwood is gentle, pretty and utterly relaxing.

The ponies keep everyone honest on pace, which suits a classic just fine. Beaulieu, home to the National Motor Museum, is a fitting destination for anyone who loves old machinery. The New Forest destination guide lists the best cafes and stops. This is the kind of ride where the bike stays cool and so do you.

Peak District Villages and Dales

Skip the busy tourist passes and the White Peak around Bakewell and Ashbourne rewards a classic beautifully. The gentler limestone lanes offer engaging but unthreatening corners, and the villages are close enough together that you never ride far without a natural stopping point. A relaxed 55-mile loop linking Bakewell, Tideswell and Ashbourne gives you drystone-walled dales, honeyed stone villages and roads that flatter rather than intimidate an older machine.

Bakewell is the obvious hub with plenty of parking and, naturally, the famous pudding. When you feel like something more dramatic on a different bike, my Peak District roads guide covers the big passes. For a classic, though, the quiet dales are the star.

Best Biker Cafes and Pubs for a Classic Day

Half the joy of a classic ride is where you stop, and Britain is blessed with cafes and pubs that welcome older machinery. Planning your route around good stops is not lazy, it is the whole point. My guides to the best biker cafes in the UK and the best biker pubs in the UK will help you build a ride around a proper brew and a plate of something hot. On a classic, the cafe is not an interruption to the ride. It is a chapter of it.

Riding a Classic Well: A Few Pointers

Older and retro machines ask a little more of you, but the rewards are worth it. Keep these in mind and the miles will be a pleasure:

  • Plan around fuel range. Many classics have modest tanks, so know where the next garage is and top up early.
  • Keep the legs short. Frequent stops suit both the machine and an upright riding position that lacks fairing protection.
  • Avoid sustained motorway. Air-cooled engines and older brakes prefer flowing A and B roads to high-speed slogs.
  • Carry a soft tank bag. Something like the Oxford Aqua T-20 Tank Bag keeps essentials handy without spoiling the lines of a classic.
  • Listen to the machine. Part of classic ownership is reading the engine. If it wants a rest, give it one.

The Best Modern Retros for These Roads

You do not need a fragile vintage machine to enjoy classic-style riding. Modern retros deliver the look and the relaxed character with the reliability to tour in confidence. The Royal Enfield Interceptor 650 is my top pick for these routes, a wonderfully honest air-and-oil-cooled twin that positively encourages a gentle pace. The Triumph Bonneville T120 brings a touch more polish and grunt while keeping the classic silhouette, and the Moto Guzzi V85 TT offers characterful retro-adventure charm for those who like a little rough with the smooth.

For a wider look at retro touring machines, see my guide to classic touring bikes. Whatever you ride, the best roads for classic motorcycles in the UK are about savouring the journey. Take it slow, stop often and let the character of the machine set the pace.

The Yorkshire Dales B6160 through Wharfedale follows the valley floor for gentle 70-mile grand touring.
The New Forest and Avon Valley (45 miles) is kind to modest brakes and drum-braked front ends.
